source.title: Information-Theoretic Foundations for Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Hong Jun Jeon; B. Van Roy

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including proofs, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives a compute-optimal allocation result using an information-theoretic upper bound for an idealized neural-network learning problem, rather than measuring language-model scaling empirically.
record.gate_note: The paper cites empirical scaling studies but reports no results from those studies as its own. Its own relevant results are theoretical bounds for reducible error and a compute-optimal allocation obtained by minimizing one such bound.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper. It bounds reducible cumulative log-loss for a Bayesian predictor on synthetic data from an infinite-width two-layer ReLU network, then minimizes that bound under a FLOP constraint. It measures no language-model loss and no actual loss optimum. The Θ̃(√C) split is the minimizer of an upper bound whose tightness is only conjectured, a related but different construct from V3's loss-minimising allocation. It argues for consistency with Hoffmann et al. rather than testing any version, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the near-linear optimal data-to-model relation corroborates large-scale empirical work, namely Hoffmann et al. They frame this as a first rigorous step that rests on an upper bound conjectured to be tight. They note it is limited to single-hidden-layer networks, pretraining compute only, and idealized Bayesian inference.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical information-theoretic derivation for synthetic binary-label data and an idealized Bayesian constrained predictor, not an empirical sweep of language models or fitted power-law extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimizing the Corollary 4.2 error upper bound under d·n·T ≤ C gives parameter count and dataset size both Θ̃(√C), i.e. a linear relation up to log factors (Theorem 4.3, Figure 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In an idealized Bayesian setting with data from an infinite-width two-layer ReLU network, the compute-optimal split that minimizes an information-theoretic error upper bound scales parameters and data equally, up to log factors.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducible error is bounded by an estimation term decaying as 1/T (log in n) plus a misspecification term decaying as K/n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the specified idealized learning problem, reducible expected log-loss is bounded by separate estimation and misspecification terms with different dependencies on data size and model width.

record.problems: The result is a theoretical upper bound rather than measured loss, and its tightness is conjectured. The analysis uses a single-hidden-layer synthetic neural-network setting and idealized Bayesian inference; the authors state that generalization to state-of-the-art architectures remains open.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported result was left out.

untested.parts: All: no measured held-out loss of language models versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no empirical or exact loss-minimising allocation. Only a bound minimizer in a toy setting.
All: no other modalities or regimes.
All: no comparison of fitting choices or curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V3 supports/limits_scope labels are rejected. The result is a bound minimizer, not a loss minimizer, in a non-language-model synthetic system. The loss is cumulative online KL-based reducible error, not held-out loss. Figure 1 (d=10, K=100) plots the bound only, so it adds no measured evidence. A reviewer who accepts theoretical derivations as T2 tests could instead link R3 to V3 as weak support. Even then, the conjectured tightness would need flagging.

Whether fits from small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
The paper minimizes an upper bound in an idealized synthetic learning problem, not measured loss in language-model runs.
Effects of varying depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether empirical fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, or whether empirical curves bend away from power laws.

It cannot show where actual loss is minimised, so it should not count as an observation of V3.
